description.value: The study investigated whether fMRI activation elicited by high-calorie food pictures predicts weight loss during a 12-week psychosocial program and weight maintenance during a 9-month follow-up in obese participants.

spans.text: We used functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to investigate activation in reward-system as well as other brain regions in response to viewing high-calorie food vs. control pictures in 25 obese individuals before and after a 12-week psychosocial weight-loss treatment and at 9-mo follow-up.

design.value: Longitudinal fMRI study with obese participants scanned before and after a 12-week behavioral psychosocial weight-loss program, with body weight assessed again at 9-month follow-up; normal-weight controls were scanned twice 12 weeks apart.

spans.text: In the present study, we used a longitudinal design to examine neural activation to food pictures in obese participants before and after a 12-wk behavioral, psychosocial weight-loss program.

Participants were scheduled for two separate fMRI imaging sessions, one within the first 3 wk of starting the EatRight program and another within 1 wk after the program ended. Control participants were also imaged twice, 12 wk apart, but did not participate in the EatRight program.
Before the scans, each participant completed a visual analog scale (VAS) measuring hunger (as in ) and detailed the time and content of their last meal.
The pre-scan mean hunger rating was 96.5 on the 0–150 VAS rating scale, and was thus generally consistent with the moderate hunger that would be experienced after an 8-h fast.

task_name.value: viewing high-calorie food vs. control pictures

spans.text: We used functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to investigate activation in reward-system as well as other brain regions in response to viewing high-calorie food vs. control pictures in 25 obese individuals before and after a 12-week psychosocial weight-loss treatment and at 9-mo follow-up.

task_description.value: Participants viewed high-calorie sweet food, high-calorie savory food, low-calorie food, and car images in six runs during pre- and post-treatment fMRI sessions.

spans.text: Each run consisted of two pseudorandomly presented epochs each of car and low-calorie food images, and one epoch each of high-calorie sweet food and high-calorie savory food images (see in ).
Visual stimuli were presented in a block design format, with a total of six 3:15 min runs for both the pre- and post-treatment scanning sessions.
The stimuli were presented by a Dell Latitude D630 laptop computer using VPM software ( ).

instructions.value: Participants were instructed to eat a normal breakfast and then refrain from eating for 8 h before being imaged; they were also instructed to abstain from alcohol for 24 h, avoid exercise on the day of the study, and avoid caffeine for 3 h prior to imaging.

spans.text: Following our standard protocol ( ), participants were instructed to eat a normal breakfast and then refrain from eating for 8 h before being imaged.
Participants were also instructed to abstain from alcohol for 24 h prior to the imaging session, to avoid exercise on the day of the study, and to avoid caffeine for 3 h prior to imaging.

stimuli.value: 504 high-quality color photographs, including high-calorie foods, low-calorie foods, and cars as control images.

spans.text: Visual stimuli consisted of 504 high-quality color photographs selected from previous studies ( ) with additional comparable photographs taken with a digital camera or scanned from popular food magazines.
The control images consisted of pictures of cars; these images were moderately engaging control stimuli that matched the low-calorie food images in ratings of pleasantness ( ).
